ANA-positive referrals with a low risk of SLE are a significant burden on secondary care and constitute up to 7% of rheumatologists’ new referral workloads. Once individuals with suspected SLE are referred to rheumatology, diagnosis remains challenging, since the cardinal symptoms or signs are usually not present at first referral.

It may be difficult for rheumatologists to confirm that potential features (eg rash) are autoimmune related without other investigations/opinions. For example, they may request a dermatology opinion and skin biopsy. Due to the complex multisystem nature of the disease, individuals with suspected SLE may require follow-up appointments and referral to different specialties for further tests and investigations.
